title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 4 - adding post-secondary
Sample: N = 22,663 | AIC: 24,968.87 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0551
Model Comparison (vs. Model 3)
Likelihood ratio test: χ²(1) = 498.15, p < 0.001 — adding attended.ps is a large, statistically significant improvement over Model 3. AIC improved from 25,465.02 → 24,968.87.
Coefficient Interpretation
Carried from Model 3

GenderF remains stable and significant (OR = 0.80, CI 0.75–0.85, p < 0.001).
RaceEthnicityAI remains significant and negative (OR = 0.46, CI 0.29–0.70).
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI is marginal (OR = 0.82, CI 0.67–1.00, p = 0.051).
RaceEthnicityBlack strengthens further (Model 3: OR = 0.51 → Model 4: OR = 0.47, CI 0.40–0.55, p < 0.001) — gap widens once attended.ps enters, replicating the Part 1 pattern at this same time point.
RaceEthnicityHispanic flips back into significance (Model 3: OR = 0.91, p = 0.115 → Model 4: OR = 0.88, CI 0.78–1.00, p = 0.044) — a reversal of the Model 3 attenuation, worth noting as an inconsistent trajectory for this variable across the sequence.
economic.status remains non-significant (OR = 1.00, CI 0.94–1.07, p = 0.996).
SpecialEdStatus attenuates (Model 3: OR = 0.69 → Model 4: OR = 0.73, CI 0.67–0.79) but remains large and significant.
english.learner remains significant and negative (OR = 0.78, CI 0.70–0.87, p < 0.001) — holding steady across all four blocks, mirroring the Part 1 pattern exactly.
Dem_DescEntirely urban remains significant (OR = 1.12, CI 1.01–1.23, p = 0.031).
Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix remains non-significant.
edrEDR 10 - Southeast remains non-significant (OR = 1.00, CI 0.93–1.07, p = 0.965).
avg.unemp.rate strengthens back into clear significance (Model 3: OR = 0.98, p = 0.059 → Model 4: OR = 0.93, CI 0.91–0.96, p < 0.001).
avg.wages.pct.state remains non-significant (OR = 0.70, CI 0.44–1.11, p = 0.127).
pseo.participant remains significant and positive (OR = 1.11, CI 1.01–1.22, p = 0.025).
took.ACTYes remains large and significant (OR = 3.02, CI 2.44–3.74, p < 0.001), essentially stable from Model 3.
ACTCompositeScore.filled remains significant and negative (OR = 0.94 per point, CI 0.93–0.95, p < 0.001).
ap.exam remains significant and negative (OR = 0.75, CI 0.66–0.85, p < 0.001).
sat.taken remains significant and negative (OR = 0.57, CI 0.35–0.88, p = 0.016).
cte.achievement categories both attenuate slightly but remain significant and large: Concentrator/Completor (OR = 1.54, CI 1.39–1.70, p < 0.001), Participant (OR = 1.27, CI 1.16–1.39, p < 0.001) — still noticeably larger than the equivalent Part 1 Model 4 coefficients (OR = 1.34 and 1.14).
total.cte.courses.taken remains stable and significant (OR = 1.03 per course, CI 1.02–1.04, p < 0.001).

New: Postsecondary Attendance

attended.psYes shows a large, highly significant positive effect (OR = 2.12, CI 1.99–2.27, p < 0.001) — similar in magnitude to the Part 1 equivalent (OR = 2.36), though slightly smaller.

Multicollinearity Check
took.ACT (3.54) and ACTCompositeScore.filled (3.66) remain elevated for the expected structural reason. attended.ps shows a low GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) (1.04) — no collinearity concern. All other variables remain within acceptable range.
Substantive Pattern
This is the final model in the Year 1/Part 2 sequence. attended.ps produces a large, independent positive effect here as well, similar in size to Part 1 — postsecondary exposure appears to matter about equally for staying somewhere in Minnesota versus staying specifically in-region. RaceEthnicityBlack’s gap widening once attended.ps enters replicates the Part 1 pattern exactly, now confirmed in both outcome specifications at Year 1. CTE achievement’s consistently larger coefficients throughout this Part 2 sequence (relative to Part 1, at every model stage) is a clean, replicated finding — CTE engagement appears to be a stronger predictor of staying specifically in-region than of the broader “in Minnesota” outcome, consistent with CTE’s typically regional/local program design. english.learner has now held a stable, significant negative association across all four model blocks in both Part 1 and Part 2 at Year 1 — this is the clearest cross-outcome replication of the “unexplained disadvantage” pattern seen anywhere in this project so far.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 1 - Demographics
Sample: N = 25,484 | AIC: 31,377.47 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0117
As expected for a demographics-only baseline, model fit is minimal here — this is the starting reference point for tracking how these coefficients move as HS characteristics and accomplishments are added in later blocks, and for comparing against Part 1 at Year 5 and against the Part 2 sequence at Year 1.
Coefficient Interpretation
Gender and Race/Ethnicity

Female non-completers show significantly lower odds of sustained regional employment at Year 5 (OR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.78–0.87) relative to male non-completers — similar in magnitude to both Part 1 at Year 5 (OR = 0.83) and Part 2 at Year 1 (OR = 0.78).
All four race/ethnicity categories are significant here. American Indian (OR = 0.49, CI 0.33–0.72), Asian/Pacific Islander (OR = 0.68, CI 0.57–0.81), Black (OR = 0.42, CI 0.36–0.48) — the largest gap seen at this baseline stage across any Part/Year combination so far — and Hispanic (OR = 0.87, CI 0.78–0.97, p = 0.011).
Notably, the Black gap here (OR = 0.42) is substantially larger than the equivalent Part 1/Year 5 gap (OR = 0.51) and the Part 2/Year 1 gap (OR = 0.51) — worth flagging as the widest Black-White disparity seen at any demographics-only baseline in this entire project.

Economic Status, SpecialEdStatus, and English Learner

Economic status is not significant (OR = 0.97, CI 0.92–1.03, p = 0.350), consistent with every other Part/Year combination so far.
SpecialEdStatus is significant (OR = 0.82, CI 0.76–0.88) — smaller in magnitude than Part 2/Year 1 (OR = 0.70) and similar to Part 1/Year 5 (OR = 0.71).
English learner is significant (OR = 0.84, CI 0.76–0.93, p = 0.001) — consistent with its pattern of early significance at Year 5 in Part 1, and with Part 2/Year 1.

Multicollinearity Check
All GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) values are low, with the highest being English learner at 1.19 and RaceEthnicity at 1.04, both well under the ~2.0–2.5 concern threshold.
Substantive Pattern
The Black-White gap here is the largest seen at any demographics-only baseline across the entire Part 1/Part 2, Year 1/5/10 matrix so far — worth watching closely whether this widens further or attenuates as later blocks are added, given how consistently this disparity has resisted attenuation elsewhere in this project. english.learner and SpecialEdStatus are both already significant at this baseline, consistent with the broader pattern that these variables tend to emerge early (or stay stable) rather than following a suppression pattern in this non-completer population.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 2 - adding high school characteristics
Sample: N = 25,484 | AIC: 31,321.55 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0138
Model Comparison (vs. Model 1)
Likelihood ratio test: χ²(5) = 65.927, p < 0.001 — Model 2 is a statistically significant improvement over Model 1. AIC improved from 31,377.47 → 31,321.55.
Coefficient Interpretation
Carried from Model 1

GenderF remains stable and significant (OR = 0.83, CI 0.78–0.87, p < 0.001).
RaceEthnicityAI remains significant and negative (OR = 0.50, CI 0.33–0.72), essentially unchanged from Model 1.
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI strengthens (Model 1: OR = 0.68 → Model 2: OR = 0.66, CI 0.55–0.78).
RaceEthnicityBlack strengthens further (Model 1: OR = 0.42 → Model 2: OR = 0.40, CI 0.34–0.46) — widening rather than narrowing, and now the largest Black-White gap seen anywhere in this project at this model stage.
RaceEthnicityHispanic remains significant (OR = 0.87, CI 0.78–0.98, p = 0.017), essentially stable.
economic.status remains non-significant (OR = 0.97, CI 0.92–1.03, p = 0.379).
SpecialEdStatus remains stable and significant (OR = 0.82, CI 0.77–0.88).
english.learner remains stable and significant (OR = 0.83, CI 0.75–0.91, p < 0.001).

High School Characteristics

Dem_DescEntirely urban is significant and positive (OR = 1.19, CI 1.09–1.29, p < 0.001).
Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix is significant and negative (OR = 0.89, CI 0.83–0.96, p = 0.003) — the first time this specific category has reached significance across any Part/Year combination so far.
edrEDR 10 - Southeast is marginal, not significant at 0.05 (OR = 1.05, CI 0.99–1.12, p = 0.093).
avg.unemp.rate is not significant (OR = 1.00, CI 0.98–1.03, p = 0.665) — different from Part 1 at Year 5, where this was significant and positive at this stage.
avg.wages.pct.state is significant and negative (OR = 0.51, CI 0.34–0.77, p = 0.001) — a large effect, and consistent with the Part 2/Year 1 pattern of this variable showing significance in Part 2 where it didn’t (or showed differently) in Part 1.

Multicollinearity Check
All GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) values remain low, with the highest being English learner at 1.19 and avg.wages.pct.state at 1.17, both well under the ~2.0–2.5 concern threshold.
Substantive Pattern
The Black-White gap widens further here rather than attenuating (OR 0.42 → 0.40), continuing to be the largest disparity of any kind seen at this model stage across the entire project. Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix reaching significance here — the first time this specific category has been significant at any Part/Year combination — is a new and notable pattern, worth watching through Model 3. avg.wages.pct.state’s significance here (as in Part 2/Year 1) reinforces the emerging pattern that this variable behaves differently across Part 1 vs. Part 2: it tends to show up as a real, significant negative predictor specifically for the “stay in-region” outcome, even where it’s null or different in the “stay in Minnesota” outcome at the same time point.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 3 - adding high school accomplishments
Sample: N = 25,484 | AIC: 30,748.57 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0324
Model Comparison (vs. Model 2)
Likelihood ratio test: χ²(8) = 588.98, p < 0.001 — Model 3 is a large, statistically significant improvement over Model 2. AIC improved from 31,321.55 → 30,748.57.
Coefficient Interpretation
Carried from Model 2

GenderF attenuates (Model 2: OR = 0.83 → Model 3: OR = 0.88, CI 0.83–0.93, p < 0.001) but remains significant and negative.
RaceEthnicityAI attenuates slightly (Model 2: OR = 0.50 → Model 3: OR = 0.52, CI 0.34–0.76) but remains significant.
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI attenuates (Model 2: OR = 0.66 → Model 3: OR = 0.72, CI 0.60–0.87) but remains significant.
RaceEthnicityBlack attenuates slightly for the first time in this sequence (Model 2: OR = 0.40 → Model 3: OR = 0.41, CI 0.35–0.47) — a marginal narrowing rather than the widening seen at other points in this project, though the gap remains the largest of any demographic variable by a wide margin.
RaceEthnicityHispanic weakens to marginal (Model 2: OR = 0.87, p = 0.017 → Model 3: OR = 0.90, CI 0.81–1.01, p = 0.078).
economic.status flips into significance (Model 2: OR = 0.97, p = 0.379 → Model 3: OR = 0.94, CI 0.88–0.99, p = 0.030) — a new, small but real disadvantage emerging once accomplishments are added, a pattern not seen in Part 1 at this same stage.
SpecialEdStatus attenuates (Model 2: OR = 0.82 → Model 3: OR = 0.79, CI 0.73–0.85) but remains significant.
english.learner strengthens further (Model 2: OR = 0.83 → Model 3: OR = 0.79, CI 0.71–0.87, p < 0.001) — consistent with the strengthening pattern seen everywhere else in this project.
Dem_DescEntirely urban strengthens (Model 2: OR = 1.19 → Model 3: OR = 1.29, CI 1.19–1.41, p < 0.001).
Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix remains significant and negative (OR = 0.92, CI 0.86–1.00, p = 0.038).
edrEDR 10 - Southeast strengthens into clear significance (Model 2: OR = 1.05, p = 0.093 → Model 3: OR = 1.09, CI 1.02–1.16, p = 0.009).
avg.unemp.rate flips into significance (Model 2: OR = 1.00, p = 0.665 → Model 3: OR = 1.03, CI 1.01–1.05, p = 0.009) — positive direction, consistent with Part 1’s Year 5 pattern.
avg.wages.pct.state remains significant and negative (OR = 0.61, CI 0.40–0.92, p = 0.019) — unlike Part 2/Year 1, where this effect did not survive the accomplishments block, here it holds.

New: High School Accomplishments

pseo.participant is marginal, not significant at 0.05 (OR = 1.07, CI 0.99–1.16, p = 0.096).
took.ACTYes is significant and positive (OR = 2.47, CI 2.04–3.00, p < 0.001) — smaller than the Part 2/Year 1 equivalent (OR = 3.07), consistent with the broader Year 1 → Year 5 fading pattern seen throughout this project.
ACTCompositeScore.filled is significant and negative (OR = 0.96 per point, CI 0.95–0.97, p < 0.001).
ap.exam is significant and negative (OR = 0.84, CI 0.75–0.93, p < 0.001).
sat.taken is significant and negative (OR = 0.52, CI 0.36–0.72, p < 0.001).
cte.achievementCTE Concentrator or Completor (OR = 1.49, CI 1.36–1.63, p < 0.001) and cte.achievementCTE Participant (OR = 1.29, CI 1.20–1.39, p < 0.001) are both significant and positive — again larger than the equivalent Part 1/Year 5 coefficients (OR = 1.31 and 1.23), continuing the Part 2 > Part 1 CTE pattern established at Year 1.
total.cte.courses.taken is significant and positive (OR = 1.03 per course, CI 1.02–1.04, p < 0.001).

Multicollinearity Check
took.ACT (3.58) and ACTCompositeScore.filled (3.75) remain elevated for the expected structural reason. All other variables remain within acceptable range.
Substantive Pattern
This is the first model stage in the entire Part 1/Part 2 project where the Black-White gap actually narrows slightly rather than staying flat or widening (Model 2 → Model 3: OR 0.40 → 0.41) — a small, marginal shift, and still by far the largest disparity in the model, but worth noting as a genuine departure from the “never attenuates” pattern established elsewhere, at least at this specific stage. avg.wages.pct.state’s continued significance here (unlike its non-survival at Part 2/Year 1’s Model 3) reinforces that this variable’s behavior isn’t fully consistent even within Part 2 across time points. The CTE achievement coefficients remain consistently larger in Part 2 than Part 1 at the same time point — now confirmed at both Year 1 and Year 5 — strengthening the case that this is a genuine, replicated pattern rather than noise. economic.status emerging as significant once accomplishments are controlled (rather than staying null throughout, as in Part 1) is a new wrinkle worth tracking into Model 4.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 4 - adding post-secondary
Sample: N = 25,484 | AIC: 30,607.71 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0369
Model Comparison (vs. Model 3)
Likelihood ratio test: χ²(1) = 142.86, p < 0.001 — adding attended.ps is a statistically significant improvement over Model 3. AIC improved from 30,748.57 → 30,607.71.
Coefficient Interpretation
Carried from Model 3

GenderF remains stable and significant (OR = 0.87, CI 0.82–0.92, p < 0.001).
RaceEthnicityAI remains significant and negative (OR = 0.53, CI 0.35–0.78).
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI remains significant (OR = 0.72, CI 0.60–0.86).
RaceEthnicityBlack strengthens once attended.ps enters (Model 3: OR = 0.41 → Model 4: OR = 0.39, CI 0.33–0.45, p < 0.001) — the gap widens again here, reverting from the marginal Model 2→3 narrowing and replicating the “widens with attended.ps” pattern seen everywhere else in this project. This is now the widest Black-White gap of any final model in the entire Part 1/Part 2 sequence.
RaceEthnicityHispanic remains significant (OR = 0.89, CI 0.79–1.00, p = 0.044).
economic.status weakens to marginal (Model 3: OR = 0.94, p = 0.030 → Model 4: OR = 0.95, CI 0.89–1.01, p = 0.079).
SpecialEdStatus attenuates slightly (Model 3: OR = 0.79 → Model 4: OR = 0.82, CI 0.76–0.88) but remains significant.
english.learner remains significant and negative (OR = 0.80, CI 0.72–0.88, p < 0.001) — holding steady across all four blocks, mirroring the pattern in every other Part/Year combination so far.
Dem_DescEntirely urban remains significant (OR = 1.27, CI 1.16–1.38, p < 0.001).
Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix remains significant and negative (OR = 0.92, CI 0.85–0.99, p = 0.025).
edrEDR 10 - Southeast remains significant (OR = 1.08, CI 1.01–1.15, p = 0.017).
avg.unemp.rate weakens to non-significance (Model 3: OR = 1.03, p = 0.009 → Model 4: OR = 1.01, CI 0.99–1.03, p = 0.359).
avg.wages.pct.state remains significant and negative (OR = 0.56, CI 0.37–0.85, p = 0.007) — holding through all four blocks in this Part 2/Year 5 sequence, unlike Part 2/Year 1 where it dropped out at Model 3.
pseo.participant remains non-significant (OR = 1.06, CI 0.98–1.15, p = 0.123).
took.ACTYes remains significant and positive (OR = 2.40, CI 1.98–2.92, p < 0.001), essentially stable from Model 3.
ACTCompositeScore.filled remains significant and negative (OR = 0.95 per point, CI 0.94–0.96, p < 0.001).
ap.exam remains significant and negative (OR = 0.82, CI 0.74–0.91, p < 0.001).
sat.taken remains significant and negative (OR = 0.53, CI 0.37–0.74, p < 0.001).
cte.achievement categories both attenuate slightly but remain significant and large: Concentrator/Completor (OR = 1.46, CI 1.33–1.59, p < 0.001), Participant (OR = 1.26, CI 1.17–1.36, p < 0.001) — still larger than the equivalent Part 1/Year 5 Model 4 coefficients (OR = 1.28 and 1.21).
total.cte.courses.taken remains stable and significant (OR = 1.03 per course, CI 1.02–1.04, p < 0.001).

New: Postsecondary Attendance

attended.psYes is significant and positive (OR = 1.42, CI 1.34–1.51, p < 0.001) — nearly identical in magnitude to the Part 1/Year 5 equivalent (OR = 1.43), continuing the pattern that attended.ps performs almost identically across Part 1 and Part 2 at the same time point, unlike CTE achievement which consistently differs between the two.

Multicollinearity Check
took.ACT (3.59) and ACTCompositeScore.filled (3.76) remain elevated for the expected structural reason. attended.ps shows a low GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) (1.07) — no collinearity concern. All other variables remain within acceptable range.
Substantive Pattern
This is the final model in the Year 5/Part 2 sequence. The Black-White gap’s marginal narrowing at Model 3 fully reverses here, once attended.ps enters — the gap is now wider than at any other point in the Year 5/Part 2 sequence (OR = 0.39) and wider than the equivalent Part 1/Year 5 final model (OR = 0.50). This is the widest Black-White gap seen in any final model across the entire project to date, and reinforces that the brief Model 2→3 narrowing was likely noise rather than a genuine pattern. avg.wages.pct.state’s persistence through all four blocks here — unlike its disappearance at Model 3 in Part 2/Year 1 — means this variable’s Part 2-specific significance is not fully consistent across time points, though it is significant in three of the four Part 1/Part 2 sequences completed so far at Year 1 and Year 5. english.learner continues its now-universal pattern of stable, unattenuated significance across every single Part/Year combination completed so far.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 1 - Demographics
Sample: N = 10,091 | AIC: 12,260.76 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0089
As expected for a demographics-only baseline, model fit is minimal here — this is the starting reference point for tracking how these coefficients move as HS characteristics and accomplishments are added in later blocks, and for comparing against Part 1 at Year 10 and against the Part 2 sequence at Years 1 and 5.
Coefficient Interpretation
Gender and Race/Ethnicity

Female non-completers show significantly lower odds of sustained regional employment at Year 10 (OR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.72–0.86) relative to male non-completers — similar in magnitude to Part 1/Year 10 (OR = 0.74).
RaceEthnicityAI is marginal, not significant at 0.05 (OR = 0.52, CI 0.25–1.00, p = 0.066) — a wide CI reflecting the small Year 10 AI cell size (n = 52) already flagged in Part 1. Direction is consistent with a real disadvantage, but this should not be treated as a confirmed finding given the sample size.
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI is significant (OR = 0.69, CI 0.50–0.92, p = 0.014).
RaceEthnicityBlack remains large and significant (OR = 0.43, CI 0.33–0.56) — consistent with the substantial, stable Black-White gap seen at every other Part/Year combination in this project.
RaceEthnicityHispanic is not significant (OR = 0.97, CI 0.81–1.17, p = 0.765) — different from Part 2/Year 1 and Year 5, where Hispanic reached significance at this same baseline stage.

Economic Status, SpecialEdStatus, and English Learner

Economic status is not significant (OR = 1.05, CI 0.96–1.16, p = 0.267).
SpecialEdStatus is not significant here (OR = 0.97, CI 0.87–1.09, p = 0.644) — a notable departure from every other Part/Year combination in this project, where SpecialEdStatus has been significant at the demographics-only baseline every time.
English learner is significant (OR = 0.77, CI 0.64–0.93, p = 0.007) — the largest english.learner effect seen at any demographics-only baseline across the entire project.

Multicollinearity Check
All GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) values are low, with the highest being English learner at 1.13 and RaceEthnicity at 1.03, both well under the ~2.0–2.5 concern threshold.
Substantive Pattern
SpecialEdStatus losing significance here is a genuine departure from its pattern everywhere else in this project — worth watching whether this holds through later blocks or whether it’s a Year 10 sample-size artifact similar to what happened with RaceEthnicityAI in Part 1. english.learner, by contrast, is stronger here than at any other baseline stage seen so far — continuing to look like the most robust, stable “unexplained disadvantage” finding in this entire non-completer analysis, right alongside the Black-White gap. RaceEthnicityHispanic’s null result here, unlike its significance in both prior Part 2 time points, is also worth tracking rather than assuming is meaningful given the smaller Year 10 sample.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 2 - adding high school characteristics
Sample: N = 10,091 | AIC: 12,241.50 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0113
Model Comparison (vs. Model 1)
Likelihood ratio test: χ²(5) = 29.261, p < 0.001 — Model 2 is a statistically significant improvement over Model 1, unlike Part 1/Year 10 at this same stage, where the equivalent block was not significant (p = 0.146).
Coefficient Interpretation
Carried from Model 1

GenderF remains stable and significant (OR = 0.79, CI 0.72–0.86, p < 0.001).
RaceEthnicityAI remains marginal (OR = 0.53, CI 0.25–1.03, p = 0.077), essentially unchanged from Model 1.
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI remains significant (OR = 0.66, CI 0.48–0.88, p = 0.006).
RaceEthnicityBlack remains large and significant (OR = 0.41, CI 0.31–0.53) — essentially stable from Model 1.
RaceEthnicityHispanic remains non-significant (OR = 0.99, CI 0.82–1.19, p = 0.916).
economic.status remains non-significant (OR = 1.06, CI 0.97–1.16, p = 0.223).
SpecialEdStatus remains non-significant (OR = 0.98, CI 0.87–1.10, p = 0.735) — continuing the pattern established at Model 1, where this variable broke from its significant pattern everywhere else in the project.
english.learner strengthens further (Model 1: OR = 0.77 → Model 2: OR = 0.75, CI 0.62–0.91, p = 0.003).

High School Characteristics

Dem_DescEntirely urban is not significant (OR = 1.06, CI 0.92–1.22, p = 0.429).
Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix is significant and negative (OR = 0.84, CI 0.75–0.95, p = 0.004) — consistent with the pattern first seen in Part 2/Year 5, where this specific category reached significance in a way it never did in Part 1.
edrEDR 10 - Southeast is not significant (OR = 1.04, CI 0.94–1.15, p = 0.427).
avg.unemp.rate is not significant (OR = 0.96, CI 0.91–1.01, p = 0.133).
avg.wages.pct.state is not significant (OR = 0.77, CI 0.39–1.51, p = 0.445) — different from both Part 2/Year 1 and Part 2/Year 5, where this reached significance at this same stage.

Multicollinearity Check
All GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) values remain low, with the highest being Dem_Desc at 1.14 and avg.unemp.rate at 1.22, both well under the ~2.0–2.5 concern threshold.
Substantive Pattern
Unlike Part 1/Year 10, where the HS-characteristics block failed to reach significance as a set, Part 2’s equivalent block is significant here — driven specifically by Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix. This is a meaningful divergence between the two outcomes at this same time point: the narrower “stay in-region” outcome retains a detectable HS-characteristics signal at Year 10 where the broader “stay in Minnesota” outcome does not. SpecialEdStatus’s continued non-significance here, now across both Model 1 and Model 2, looks increasingly like a genuine Year 10 pattern specific to this variable rather than a one-off, though it’s still worth a cell-size check given the smaller Year 10 sample overall. avg.wages.pct.state losing significance here, after being significant at both Part 2/Year 1 and Part 2/Year 5, likely reflects the same reduced-power dynamic already discussed for Part 1/Year 10.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 3 - adding high school accomplishments
Sample: N = 10,091 | AIC: 12,030.52 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0297
Model Comparison (vs. Model 2)
Likelihood ratio test: χ²(8) = 226.981, p < 0.001 — Model 3 is a large, statistically significant improvement over Model 2. AIC improved from 12,241.50 → 12,030.52.
Coefficient Interpretation
Carried from Model 2

GenderF attenuates (Model 2: OR = 0.79 → Model 3: OR = 0.85, CI 0.77–0.93, p < 0.001) but remains significant and negative.
RaceEthnicityAI weakens further to non-significance (Model 2: OR = 0.53, p = 0.077 → Model 3: OR = 0.56, CI 0.26–1.08, p = 0.102), continuing the pattern seen in Part 1/Year 10, very likely attributable to the small cell size (n = 52).
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI weakens to marginal (Model 2: OR = 0.66, p = 0.006 → Model 3: OR = 0.74, CI 0.54–1.00, p = 0.055).
RaceEthnicityBlack remains large and significant (OR = 0.40, CI 0.31–0.52) — essentially unchanged from Model 2, and continuing to be the largest disparity of any kind in this Year 10/Part 2 sequence.
RaceEthnicityHispanic remains non-significant (OR = 1.03, CI 0.85–1.24, p = 0.759).
economic.status remains non-significant (OR = 1.00, CI 0.91–1.10, p = 0.944).
SpecialEdStatus remains non-significant (OR = 0.93, CI 0.82–1.05, p = 0.226) — now non-significant across all three models in this sequence, continuing the departure from the pattern seen everywhere else in this project.
english.learner strengthens further (Model 2: OR = 0.75 → Model 3: OR = 0.72, CI 0.59–0.86, p < 0.001) — now the strongest english.learner effect seen at any model stage across the entire project.
Dem_DescEntirely urban remains non-significant (OR = 1.11, CI 0.96–1.28, p = 0.156).
Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix strengthens and remains significant (Model 2: OR = 0.84 → Model 3: OR = 0.82, CI 0.73–0.92, p = 0.001).
edrEDR 10 - Southeast remains non-significant (OR = 1.07, CI 0.96–1.18, p = 0.215).
avg.unemp.rate is marginal, not significant at 0.05 (OR = 0.95, CI 0.90–1.00, p = 0.065).
avg.wages.pct.state remains non-significant (OR = 0.57, CI 0.29–1.15, p = 0.115).

New: High School Accomplishments

pseo.participant is not significant (OR = 1.03, CI 0.90–1.18, p = 0.632).
took.ACTYes is significant and positive (OR = 2.41, CI 1.64–3.53, p < 0.001) — notably larger than the equivalent Part 1/Year 10 coefficient (OR = 1.74), breaking from the otherwise consistent pattern of Part 2 CTE effects being larger while ACT-related effects had tracked similarly between the two outcomes at earlier time points.
ACTCompositeScore.filled is significant and negative (OR = 0.96 per point, CI 0.94–0.97, p < 0.001).
ap.exam is significant and negative (OR = 0.81, CI 0.68–0.95, p = 0.013) — different from Part 1/Year 10, where this was non-significant at this same stage.
sat.taken is significant and negative (OR = 0.38, CI 0.21–0.63, p < 0.001) — the largest sat.taken effect (in either direction) seen anywhere in this entire project.
cte.achievementCTE Concentrator or Completor (OR = 1.55, CI 1.35–1.77, p < 0.001) and cte.achievementCTE Participant (OR = 1.27, CI 1.13–1.42, p < 0.001) are both significant and positive — continuing the pattern of larger CTE effects in Part 2 than Part 1 at every time point.
total.cte.courses.taken is significant and positive (OR = 1.03 per course, CI 1.01–1.04, p = 0.002).

Multicollinearity Check
took.ACT (4.31) and ACTCompositeScore.filled (4.50) are the most elevated of any Part/Year combination in the entire project, consistent with the smaller Year 10 sample amplifying this structural relationship. All other variables remain within acceptable range.
Substantive Pattern
sat.taken’s effect here (OR = 0.38) is the largest in either direction seen anywhere in this project, worth flagging given the likely small SAT-taking subgroup in this already-reduced Year 10 sample — a cell-size check would be worth doing before treating this specific magnitude as fully stable. SpecialEdStatus’s continued non-significance across all three models in this sequence is now a consistent pattern specific to Year 10/Part 2, reinforcing the possibility that this is a genuine Year 10 finding rather than noise, though it’s still worth weighing against the smaller sample. english.learner continues to strengthen and is now stronger here than in any other Part/Year combination in the entire project — alongside the Black-White gap, this looks like the most robust “unexplained disadvantage” finding across the whole non-completer analysis.

text:
Model 4 - adding post-secondary
Sample: N = 10,091 | AIC: 12,009.58 | Pseudo R² (McFadden-style): 0.0315
Model Comparison (vs. Model 3)
Likelihood ratio test: χ²(1) = 22.941, p < 0.001 — adding attended.ps is a statistically significant improvement over Model 3. AIC improved from 12,030.52 → 12,009.58.
Coefficient Interpretation
Carried from Model 3

GenderF remains stable and significant (OR = 0.84, CI 0.76–0.92, p < 0.001).
RaceEthnicityAI remains non-significant (OR = 0.57, CI 0.27–1.10, p = 0.113), consistent with the small cell size (n = 52).
RaceEthnicityAsian/PI remains marginal (OR = 0.74, CI 0.54–1.00, p = 0.056).
RaceEthnicityBlack strengthens once attended.ps enters (Model 3: OR = 0.40 → Model 4: OR = 0.39, CI 0.30–0.50, p < 0.001) — gap widens again, replicating the pattern seen at every other Part/Year combination in this project.
RaceEthnicityHispanic remains non-significant (OR = 1.03, CI 0.85–1.24, p = 0.784).
economic.status remains non-significant (OR = 1.00, CI 0.91–1.10, p = 0.975).
SpecialEdStatus remains non-significant (OR = 0.95, CI 0.84–1.07, p = 0.387) — non-significant across all four models in this sequence, the only Part/Year combination where this variable never reaches significance.
english.learner remains significant and negative (OR = 0.73, CI 0.60–0.88, p = 0.001) — holding steady, and still the strongest english.learner effect of any Part/Year combination at this final model stage.
Dem_DescEntirely urban remains non-significant (OR = 1.09, CI 0.94–1.26, p = 0.245).
Dem_DescUrban/town/rural mix remains significant and negative (OR = 0.81, CI 0.72–0.92, p < 0.001).
edrEDR 10 - Southeast remains non-significant (OR = 1.05, CI 0.95–1.17, p = 0.312).
avg.unemp.rate strengthens into significance (Model 3: OR = 0.95, p = 0.065 → Model 4: OR = 0.94, CI 0.89–1.00, p = 0.040).
avg.wages.pct.state is marginal, not significant at 0.05 (OR = 0.55, CI 0.27–1.10, p = 0.088).
pseo.participant remains non-significant (OR = 1.03, CI 0.90–1.18, p = 0.649).
took.ACTYes remains significant and positive (OR = 2.19, CI 1.49–3.23, p < 0.001), essentially stable from Model 3.
ACTCompositeScore.filled remains significant and negative (OR = 0.96 per point, CI 0.94–0.98, p < 0.001).
ap.exam remains significant and negative (OR = 0.81, CI 0.68–0.96, p = 0.013).
sat.taken remains significant and negative (OR = 0.38, CI 0.21–0.63, p < 0.001) — stable from Model 3, still the largest effect of any kind seen anywhere in the project.
cte.achievement categories both remain significant: Concentrator/Completor (OR = 1.53, CI 1.33–1.75, p < 0.001), Participant (OR = 1.25, CI 1.11–1.40, p < 0.001) — continuing the pattern of larger CTE effects in Part 2 than Part 1 at every time point.
total.cte.courses.taken remains stable and significant (OR = 1.03 per course, CI 1.01–1.04, p = 0.001).

New: Postsecondary Attendance

attended.psYes is significant and positive (OR = 1.26, CI 1.14–1.38, p < 0.001) — similar in magnitude to the Part 1/Year 10 equivalent (OR = 1.28), continuing the pattern that attended.ps performs almost identically across Part 1 and Part 2 at the same time point.

Multicollinearity Check
took.ACT (4.33) and ACTCompositeScore.filled (4.50) remain the most elevated of any Part/Year combination in the project, consistent with Model 3. attended.ps shows a low GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) (1.08) — no collinearity concern. All other variables remain within acceptable range.
Substantive Pattern
This is the final model in the Year 10/Part 2 sequence, and the last model in the full Part 1/Part 2 matrix. RaceEthnicityBlack’s gap widens once more with attended.ps, now confirmed at all six Part/Year combinations completed in this project — a fully universal pattern. english.learner remains the strongest, most consistent unexplained disadvantage of any demographic variable across the whole non-completer analysis, holding significant at every single model in every single Part/Year combination without exception. SpecialEdStatus’s non-significance across all four models here is now a clean, complete departure from its otherwise universal significance pattern everywhere else in this project — this looks like a genuine Year 10/Part 2-specific finding rather than noise, given it held up (weakly) in Part 1/Year 10 at the same time point but not here.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Framing and Interpretation
This methodology prioritizes a trajectory-based understanding of workforce participation, recognizing that early-career labor market experiences are dynamic rather than static. By combining persistence measures, regional employment location, and job-holding intensity, the analysis aims to provide actionable insights for workforce development and labor force planning in Southeast Minnesota.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Data Prep

non_sustained.level <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  mutate(non_sustained = ifelse(states == "Non-sustained WF", "Non-sustained", "Other"),
         non_sustained = as.factor(non_sustained)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, non_sustained) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, non_sustained, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  filter(non_sustained == "Non-sustained") %>%
  mutate(non_sustained.cat = ifelse(n == 0, "Never non-sustained",
                                    ifelse(n %in% c(1,2), "Intermittently non-sustained",
                                           ifelse(n == 3, "Broadly non-sustained",
                                                  ifelse(n %in% c(4,5), "Persistently non-sustained", "A")))),
         non_sustained.cat = fct_relevel(non_sustained.cat, "Never non-sustained", "Intermittently non-sustained", "Broadly non-sustained", "Persistently non-sustained"))

no_record.level <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  mutate(no_record = ifelse(states == "No MN emp record", "No record", "Other"),
         no_record = as.factor(no_record)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, no_record) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, no_record, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  filter(no_record == "No record") %>%
  mutate(no_record.cat = ifelse(n == 0, "Never no-record",
                                ifelse(n %in% c(1,2), "Intermittently no-record",
                                       ifelse(n == 3, "Broadly no-record",
                                              ifelse(n %in% c(4,5), "Persistently no-record", "A")))),
         no_record.cat = fct_relevel(no_record.cat, "Never no-record", "Intermittently no-record", "Broadly no-record", "Persistently no-record"))

master.sep <- Master.annual.wf.states.disconnected %>%
  left_join(non_sustained.level, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(no_record.level, by = "PersonID") %>%
  rename(non.sustained.n = n.x,
         no.record.n = n.y)

write_csv(master.sep, "Data/Claude/Non-college deeper/master-separated.csv")

Interpretation
Once isolated from “No MN employment record,” non-sustained employment on its own shows a very different shape than the original blended disconnected.cat variable. Here, the two largest categories are Never non-sustained (34.8%) and Intermittently non-sustained (39.6%) — together nearly three-quarters (74.4%) of the population. Broadly and Persistently non-sustained are much smaller and nearly equal in size (12.5% and 13.1%, respectively), together accounting for only about 25.6%.
This is a sharp contrast with the original blended distribution, where “Persistently disconnected” was the single largest category at 46.5%. Once no-record years are pulled out, persistent non-sustained employment specifically (4–5 years) drops to just 13.1% — suggesting that a large share of what was driving the original “Persistently disconnected” figure was the no-record component, not unstable employment as such.
Substantive Pattern
This confirms the value of separating the two constructs. Most non-completers who experience any non-sustained employment experience it only intermittently (1–2 years) rather than persistently — genuine long-term instability in employment itself (as opposed to absence from the record) appears to affect roughly 1 in 4 non-completers (Broad + Persistent combined), not the roughly 46% implied by the blended category. This reframes the earlier finding: persistent workforce detachment in this population looks like it’s driven more by disappearance from Minnesota’s employment record than by cycling through unstable jobs. The next table (no_record.persistence.cat) should make this contrast concrete — I’d expect that distribution to look much more like the original blended one, given how dominant “No MN record” was in the year-by-year and refined tables.

Interpretation
The no-record distribution has a different shape from both the blended category and the non-sustained-only category. A majority (56.0%) never have a “No MN employment record” year at all — larger than the “Never” share for non-sustained employment (34.8%). At the same time, Persistently no-record (21.1%) is larger than Persistently non-sustained (13.1%) — so while more people avoid no-record status entirely, those who do experience it persistently make up a larger share than persistent non-sustained employment does.
This makes the no-record distribution more bimodal than the non-sustained distribution: most people either never experience it (56.0%) or experience it persistently (21.1%), with comparatively few landing in the intermittent (17.0%) or broad (6.0%) middle categories — together only 23.0%. Non-sustained employment, by contrast, was more continuous, with Intermittent as its single largest category (39.6%).
Substantive Pattern — a correction to my earlier framing
Comparing all three tables together changes the story I gave in my previous message, and it’s worth stating clearly: I had suggested the original blended “Persistently disconnected” figure (46.5%) was being driven mainly by the no-record component. That doesn’t hold up — persistent no-record alone is only 21.1%, and persistent non-sustained alone is only 13.1%. Neither component individually gets close to explaining a 46.5% blended “persistent” rate.
What this actually implies is that a substantial share of people counted as “Persistently disconnected” in the original blended measure are experiencing a mix of non-sustained and no-record years across the 5-year window — some years unstably employed, other years absent from the record entirely — rather than being persistently stuck in one single state. That’s a more interesting and more useful finding than either component distribution shows on its own: workforce disconnection in this population isn’t just “unstable employment” or “absence from the record” as separate, stable trajectories — for a meaningful share of people, it’s a genuine back-and-forth between the two.
This makes the case for the 4×4 cross-tab of non_sustained.cat × no_record.cat even stronger than before — that table would show directly how much overlap exists between the two constructs and could confirm or disconfirm this “switching between states” interpretation with actual joint distribution numbers, rather than inference from the marginals alone.

Decomposing “Persistently Disconnected” by Driver (N = 18,063)
The table below showsonly the people who fall into “Persistently disconnected” under our original combined measure — meaning across their 5 years, they were disconnected (non-sustained OR no-record, in any mix) in 4 or 5 of those years.
The categories are defined as;

“Non-sustained driven” = this person’s disconnected years were mostly/entirely unstable employment (non-sustained), not disappearing from the record. Example: someone with 4 years of non-sustained work and 0 years of no-record. They were disconnected in the combined sense, but they were always at least working, just not steadily.
“No-record driven” = the opposite — this person’s disconnected years were mostly/entirely no employment record at all, not instability. Example: someone with 0 years non-sustained and 4 years no-record. They weren’t cycling through shaky jobs; they mostly just weren’t showing up in Minnesota’s system at all.
“Mixed (neither individually persistent)” = this person doesn’t have 4+ years in either single category, but their two counts still add up to 4 or 5 disconnected years total. Example: 2 years non-sustained + 2 years no-record = 4 disconnected years total (enough to be “persistently disconnected” overall), but only 2 in each — not enough on its own to count as “persistent” in either individual measure. This person alternated between the two problems rather than being stuck in one.

Interpretation
Among those who are persistently disconnected overall, No-record driven is the largest single group (45.3%) — nearly half of everyone in this category is disconnected primarily because they disappear from Minnesota’s employment record, not because they cycle through unstable jobs. Non-sustained driven is smaller (28.1%), and Mixed is close behind at 26.6%.
This resolves the open question from the previous table cleanly. Note that the n’s here confirm exactly: 6,921 No-record driven matches the full Persistently no-record count from the prior table, and 4,301 Non-sustained driven matches the full Persistently non-sustained count — meaning every person who is persistent in either individual measure is, by definition, also persistently disconnected overall (which makes sense, since 4+ years in either category alone guarantees 4+ combined years). The Mixed category (4,064) is the genuinely new information this table adds: it isolates the subgroup that doesn’t show up as “persistent” in either individual measure, but still accumulates enough combined disconnected years to count as persistently disconnected overall.
Substantive Pattern
This confirms and sharpens the “switching between states” interpretation I raised in my previous message, but refines it: switching between the two problems is real and sizable (26.6% of the persistently disconnected group), but it is not the dominant story — it’s the smallest of the three drivers, not the largest. The dominant story is that persistent disconnection in this population is most often a single, consistent problem rather than an alternating one, and specifically, it’s more often driven by absence from the employment record (45.3%) than by employment instability (28.1%).
This is a meaningful correction to keep in mind for how “persistent disconnection” gets framed going forward: it is not primarily a story of people bouncing between shaky jobs and gaps in the record. It’s more accurately a story where, if someone is persistently disconnected, the single most likely reason is that they’ve largely stopped appearing in Minnesota’s workforce system at all — which raises the same open question flagged earlier (and still unresolved): whether “No MN employment record” reflects leaving the state, exiting the labor force entirely, informal/unreported work, or some mix that this data can’t distinguish. That distinction matters a great deal here, since it’s now confirmed to be the single largest driver of the single largest disconnection category in this entire analysis.

    non_sustained.cat == "Persistently non-sustained" & no_record.cat == "Persistently no-record" ~ "Both persistent",
    TRUE ~ "Mixed (neither individually persistent)"
  )) %>%
  group_by(driver) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Full Summary: Descriptive Statistics on Workforce Disconnection Non-College Graduates, Southeast Minnesota (Years 1–5 Post-Exit)
text:
Full Summary: Descriptive Statistics on Workforce Disconnection Non-College Graduates, Southeast Minnesota (Years 1–5 Post-Exit)
Overview
Sample: N = 32,878 non-completers, tracked annually across the first five years after exiting formal education (high school or postsecondary attendance, whichever is later). This descriptive stage moved through five successive tables, each refining the picture of what “workforce disconnection” actually consists of in this population.
Step 1: The headline number — disconnection is not a marginal outcome
Using the original blended definition (disconnected = non-sustained employment OR no MN record, in a given year), 46.5% of this population is Persistently disconnected (4–5 of 5 years), far larger than any other category (Intermittently disconnected: 25.6%; Broadly disconnected: 11.7%; Consistently attached: only 16.2%). This established the core framing for the whole analysis: persistent disconnection is close to the modal outcome for non-completers in this region, not a small at-risk subgroup.
Step 2: The annual trajectory — a sorting process, not stability
Looking year-by-year, two categories grow steadily and converge: Sustained WF – SE (24.9% → 30.5%) and No MN employment record (25.9% → 30.6%) end Year 5 at nearly identical size, together accounting for over 61% of the population. Every non-sustained subtype shrinks over the same window, most sharply for “mixed” and “in-region only” statuses. This suggested a sorting dynamic: people in unstable employment situations in Year 1 gradually resolve into one of two stable poles — sustained employment or disappearance from the record — rather than remaining in an unstable middle state.
Step 3: The refined breakdown — confirms the sorting story, adds one precise number
Disaggregating “non-sustained” into simultaneous/sequential/unclassified subtypes didn’t surface a new pattern — all the granular mixed categories are small and decline together at similar rates. What it did confirm precisely: within the subset of people who are not sustainably employed, “No MN record” grows from a plurality (39.6%) in Year 1 to a clear majority (56.5%) by Year 5. This sharpened, rather than changed, the Step 2 finding.
Step 4: Splitting the construct — the two problems have different shapes, and neither explains the blended number alone
Separating “non-sustained persistence” from “no-record persistence” as two independent 5-year measures showed they behave differently: non-sustained persistence is more continuous (Intermittent is the largest category, 39.6%; only 13.1% are Persistently non-sustained), while no-record persistence is more bimodal (56.0% Never vs. 21.1% Persistently, with a small middle). Critically, neither component’s “Persistent” share (13.1% and 21.1%) comes close to explaining the original blended 46.5% Persistently disconnected figure on its own — which meant a real question remained about how people were accumulating enough combined disconnected years to land in that blended category.
Step 5: The driver breakdown — resolves the question, and revises the initial “switching” hypothesis
Among people who are persistently disconnected overall, the driver breakdown showed: No-record driven (45.3%) > Non-sustained driven (28.1%) > Mixed/switching between the two (26.6%). This confirmed that persistent disconnection is most often a single, consistent problem rather than people alternating between instability and absence — and that when it is a single problem, it’s disproportionately absence from the employment record rather than unstable employment.
What the descriptive stage is telling us, overall

Persistent disconnection is common, not rare — it’s close to a plurality outcome for non-completers in this population, not a tail-end risk group.
“Disconnection” is not one thing. Unstable employment and absence from Minnesota’s employment record behave as genuinely distinct trajectories with different shapes (continuous vs. bimodal) and different persistence rates — collapsing them into a single blended measure, as the original framing did, obscures more than it reveals.
Absence from the record, not employment instability, is the dominant driver of persistent disconnection in this population, both in the year-by-year trajectory data (Step 2/3) and in the direct driver breakdown (Step 5).
There is a real “switching” subgroup, but it’s the smallest of the three driver types (26.6%) — worth tracking in Step 3’s bivariate work, but not the central story.

Summary: Bivariate Predictors of Overall Disconnection Persistence (disconnected.cat)
Overview
This stage examined the bivariate relationship between disconnection persistence category (Consistently attached / Intermittently / Broadly / Persistently disconnected) and sixteen individual characteristics across four groups: demographics, high school characteristics, high school academics, and postsecondary attendance. Cross-tabulations with Cramér’s V were used for categorical predictors; one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc comparisons for continuous predictors. Consistent with the emphasis on substantive interpretation over significance alone, effect sizes varied enormously across groups — from negligible (high school characteristics) to the strongest relationship found anywhere in this analysis (postsecondary attendance).

(pseo.participant, MCA.R, MCA.S, avg.unemp.rate, avg.wages.pct.state either not significant or negligible — see below)
The four headline findings
1. Postsecondary exposure — even without completion — is the single strongest predictor found in this entire bivariate stage. attended.ps (V = 0.182) exceeds every other variable by a wide margin, nearly double the next-strongest relationship. This directly replicates the largest effect found throughout the earlier non-completer regression work, now confirmed using a full 5-year persistence outcome rather than a single time point.
2. CTE engagement is the second-clearest story, and unusually strong at the bivariate level. Both total.cte.courses.taken (η² ≈ 2.2%, the single strongest continuous relationship) and cte.achievement (V = 0.098) show clean, monotonic, dose-response patterns — more CTE engagement, by either measure, consistently predicts less disconnection. This is consistent with CTE’s role throughout the entire project (DV1–DV5, and both Parts of the non-completer regression work) as one of the most durable positive predictors of workforce attachment.
3. Race/ethnicity shows the largest raw disparities in the entire analysis, despite the lowest standardized effect size among demographic variables. American Indian graduates show a 21.2-point gap in persistent disconnection relative to White graduates (66.0% vs. 44.8%), and Black graduates show an 18.0-point gap (62.8%) — both larger than any other raw gap in the demographic set. This directly parallels the unexplained Black-White (and here, especially American Indian) gap that ran through the DV1, DV2, and DV5 multivariate work on completers, now confirmed at the purely bivariate level in a population that never completed any postsecondary credential — this disparity is not specific to the postsecondary pathway.
4. Academic achievement measures split into two opposing camps, and this split is genuinely new to this project. ACT composite score, SAT-taking, and AP exam participation all point toward more disconnection among higher scorers/participants, while MCA scores point toward less. This is the first time in the whole body of work (completer regressions, non-completer regressions, and now this bivariate stage) that “academic strength” measures have split so cleanly in opposite directions rather than moving together. It likely reflects something specific about non-completers who show strong test performance but never finish a credential — this subgroup may face a distinct set of risks not captured elsewhere in this analysis.
Where the signal is weak or absent
High school characteristics (Dem_Desc, edr, avg.unemp.rate, avg.wages.pct.state) show uniformly negligible relationships with disconnection category — the weakest group in this entire analysis by a wide margin, in sharp contrast to the demographic and academic groups. PSEO participation and two of the three MCA subjects (MCA.R weakly, MCA.S not at all) also show minimal-to-no bivariate relationship, a notable departure from PSEO’s stronger role in the completer-population regression work.
Connecting back to the rest of the project
This bivariate stage largely reinforces two of the most important findings from the entire body of work to date: the outsized importance of any postsecondary exposure (echoing attended.ps and ps.grad throughout the regression models) and the persistent, unexplained racial disparity — especially for American Indian and Black graduates — that shows up regardless of population (completers or non-completers), regardless of outcome (employment attachment, credential completion, or disconnection persistence), and regardless of analytic method (multivariate logistic regression or simple bivariate cross-tabulation. The one genuinely new finding is the academic-achievement split (ACT/SAT/AP vs. MCA), which hasn’t appeared in this form anywhere else in the project and is worth flagging as a distinct area for further exploration rather than folding into the existing “two forces” or “unexplained disparity” narratives.
Open items carried forward
The ap.exam and sat.taken counterintuitive directions, and the MCA-vs-ACT/SAT split, remain unexplained at the bivariate level — these associations may offer exactly the kind of clue you mentioned earlier that could shed light on what “No MN employment record” represents, once compared against the persistent non-sustained employment breakdown coming next.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Demographic variables
Overall pattern across all six variables — and a striking shift from the blended disconnected.cat results
All six relationships remain statistically significant, but the pattern of which variables are strong has shifted substantially now that non-sustained employment is isolated from no-record status. Some variables (Gender, Economic status) hold roughly steady or even strengthen; others (English learner, Non-English home, RaceEthnicity) weaken dramatically, in several cases losing most of the raw gap that made them so prominent in the blended analysis. This divergence is the most important finding in this table — it starts to answer the open question about what’s driving disconnection for different groups.
Gender (χ² = 272.661, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.091)
Female graduates show notably higher persistent non-sustained employment (15.5% vs. 11.4%, a 4.1-point gap) and much lower “Never non-sustained” rates (31.0% vs. 37.5%, a 6.5-point gap) than male graduates. This is the strongest relationship in this table, and notably, Gender’s Cramér’s V increased relative to the blended disconnected.cat result (0.074 → 0.091) — the opposite of what happened to several other variables here. This suggests the gender disadvantage in workforce disconnection is concentrated specifically in employment instability, not in disappearing from the record.
Economic Status (χ² = 216.948, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.081)
Economically disadvantaged students show higher persistent non-sustained employment (15.2% vs. 11.6%, a 3.6-point gap). Cramér’s V here (0.081) is essentially unchanged from the blended result (0.070) — if anything, slightly stronger — suggesting economic status’s disconnection effect operates fairly evenly across both non-sustained employment and no-record status, unlike several other variables in this set.
SpecialEdStatus (χ² = 192.125, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.076)
Students with SpecialEd status show higher persistent non-sustained employment (17.8% vs. 11.7%, a 6.1-point gap) — the largest raw gap of any variable in this table. However, Cramér’s V dropped meaningfully from the blended result (0.113 → 0.076), and the “Never non-sustained” rates are nearly identical between groups (33.5% vs. 35.2%) — suggesting SpecialEdStatus’s overall disconnection effect is partly, but not entirely, about employment instability specifically.
English Learner Status (χ² = 131.161, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.063)
This shows a dramatic weakening relative to the blended result. The persistent non-sustained gap is now just 2.4 points (15.2% vs. 12.8%), compared to a 13.9-point gap in the blended disconnected.cat table. Even more tellingly, English learners are now more likely to be “Never non-sustained” than non-learners (41.4% vs. 34.0%) — the opposite direction from what the blended category showed. This strongly suggests English learners’ overall disconnection disadvantage is concentrated almost entirely in disappearing from Minnesota’s employment record, not in cycling through unstable jobs.
Non-English Home (χ² = 124.025, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.061)
An even more striking version of the same pattern. The persistent non-sustained gap essentially vanishes and reverses (12.3% vs. 13.2% — non-English home students are marginally less likely to be persistently non-sustained), while “Never non-sustained” is far higher for this group (43.4% vs. 33.9%). Recall this variable showed the second-largest raw gap in the entire blended analysis (14.5 points). That gap has now almost entirely disappeared once non-sustained employment is isolated — this is close to definitive evidence that non-English-home students’ disconnection is driven almost exclusively by no-record status.
RaceEthnicity (χ² = 196.443, df = 12, Cramér’s V = 0.045)
The most dramatic shift of all six variables. In the blended table, American Indian graduates showed a 21.2-point gap in persistent disconnection relative to White graduates — here, the gap in persistent non-sustained employment is only 2.3 points (15.1% vs. 12.8%). Black graduates’ gap similarly shrinks from 18.0 points (blended) to 7.8 points (non-sustained only) — still real, but less than half its previous size. This is a significant finding: the large racial disparities that stood out so clearly in the blended disconnection measure appear to be driven substantially — for American Indian graduates, almost entirely — by no-record status rather than employment instability.

Substantive Pattern
This table provides the clearest evidence yet on the open question flagged earlier: several of the demographic disparities that looked large in the blended disconnection measure — especially RaceEthnicity (particularly American Indian), English learner status, and Non-English home — are substantially or almost entirely driven by no-record status, not by cycling through unstable employment. By contrast, Gender and Economic status show the opposite pattern: their disconnection effects hold steady or even strengthen when non-sustained employment is isolated, suggesting these two variables operate more through genuine employment instability.
This is a meaningful, substantive finding on its own, and it sets up a clear prediction for the next table: I’d expect the no-record persistence cross-tabs to show larger gaps for RaceEthnicity, English learner, and Non-English home than what appeared here, and smaller or reversed gaps for Gender and Economic status. Worth testing that prediction directly once you share the no-record table.

section: Summary: Bivariate Predictors of Non-Sustained Employment Persistence (non_sustained.cat)
text:
Summary: Bivariate Predictors of Non-Sustained Employment Persistence (non_sustained.cat)
Overview
This stage repeated the full Step 3 bivariate analysis using non_sustained.cat — employment instability persistence, isolated from no-record status — as the outcome, in place of the blended disconnected.cat measure used previously. The central purpose was to test whether the strong relationships found in the blended analysis were driven by employment instability, by no-record status, or both. The results are decisive: most variables that showed strong blended-table relationships weakened substantially or lost significance entirely once isolated to non-sustained employment specifically — but a distinct minority of variables held steady or even strengthened, and that split is itself the most important finding of this stage.

This is the majority pattern across the whole analysis — twelve of sixteen variables examined show this shape. Race/ethnicity is the most consequential example: American Indian graduates’ 21.2-point blended gap shrinks to 2.3 points once isolated to non-sustained employment, and English learner’s 13.9-point gap shrinks to 2.4 points. These findings indicate that for these groups, the blended “disconnection” story was overwhelmingly a story about disappearing from Minnesota’s employment record, not about cycling through unstable jobs.

Gender is the clearest example of a variable whose disconnection effect operates specifically through employment instability rather than record absence — its standardized effect actually grows once isolated. MCA.S is the most striking reversal in the entire analysis: completely null in the blended measure, but a clean, fully monotonic, highly significant predictor of non-sustained employment specifically. This means the blended measure was fully masking a real relationship for this variable — the opposite problem from what happened to ACT score, CTE, and SAT.
The clearest overall finding
Two genuinely distinct mechanisms are operating in this population, and this table set is the first place in the whole analysis where they can be cleanly separated:

A “record-absence” cluster: postsecondary exposure (attended.ps), CTE engagement (both measures), ACT/SAT performance, race/ethnicity, English learner and non-English home status, and local geography/economy variables all relate mainly to whether someone shows up in Minnesota’s employment system at all, not to whether their employment, once present, is stable.
A “genuine instability” cluster: Gender, Economic status, and — surprisingly — MCA Science and Reading scores (but not composite ACT) relate specifically to employment instability itself, largely independent of record-presence.

pseo.participant and took.ACT deserve a specific note: both show a complex, non-monotonic shape here — participants/test-takers are less likely to be “Never non-sustained” but not less likely to be “Persistently non-sustained,” suggesting these variables shift people from stability into occasional instability without protecting against the most severe, persistent form of it. This is a different shape from every other variable examined and doesn’t fit neatly into either cluster above.
Connecting back to the open question
This entire table set is the strongest evidence yet on what “No MN employment record” represents. If record-absence is disproportionately tied to CTE/ACT/postsecondary exposure, race/ethnicity, and English learner/non-English-home status — while genuine employment instability is tied more to Gender, Economic status, and MCA performance — that’s a meaningful clue rather than a resolved answer: it suggests “no record” may be capturing something like out-of-state migration or a shift to non-covered/informal work among people who otherwise show markers of academic engagement or are part of specific demographic groups, while genuine cycling through unstable jobs looks more tied to structural economic disadvantage and gender. This is exactly the kind of pattern-based clue you anticipated earlier — worth carrying forward as a working hypothesis, not a conclusion, once the no-record persistence tables are run and can be compared directly against this one.
Bottom line
The single most important finding from this stage: disconnection in this population is not one phenomenon with many correlates — it is (at least) two distinct phenomena with substantially different correlates, and the original decision to split disconnected.cat into non_sustained.cat and no_record.cat was analytically necessary to see this. The next step — running the same sixteen variables against no_record.cat — should now be treated as close to confirmatory rather than exploratory, given how clearly this table set has already outlined what that comparison is likely to show.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Demographic variables
Overall pattern — this table confirms the predictions from the non-sustained analysis directly
This table lets us close the loop opened by the last two tables. The prediction was that variables whose blended effect weakened when isolated to non-sustained employment should now show stronger relationships here, and vice versa. That prediction holds cleanly for four of the six variables, with two genuinely interesting exceptions.
English Learner Status (χ² = 378.567, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.107)
This is now the strongest relationship in this table, and it confirms the prediction almost perfectly. Persistent no-record: 33.4% for English learners vs. 19.5% for non-learners — a 13.9-point gap, nearly identical to the original blended gap (13.9 points) and far larger than the 2.4-point gap found for non-sustained employment specifically. This is close to definitive: English learner status’s entire disconnection disadvantage runs through no-record status, essentially none of it through employment instability.
Non-English Home (χ² = 342.585, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.102)
Nearly as clean a confirmation. Persistent no-record: 33.5% vs. 19.7% — a 13.8-point gap, almost exactly matching the original blended gap (14.5 points), and vastly larger than the non-sustained-only gap (which had nearly vanished, 12.3% vs. 13.2%). Combined with English learner status above, this table confirms that both of these related variables’ disconnection stories are overwhelmingly about record-absence, not job instability.
RaceEthnicity (χ² = 252.101, df = 12, Cramér’s V = 0.051)
A more nuanced picture than the two variables above. American Indian graduates show a persistent no-record rate of 34.4% vs. 19.8% for White graduates — a 14.6-point gap, which accounts for the large majority (about two-thirds) of AI’s original 21.2-point blended gap, with the remaining share falling in the non-sustained table (2.3 points). Black graduates show a smaller no-record gap (24.8% vs. 19.8%, 5.0 points) that’s roughly comparable in size to their non-sustained gap (7.8 points, from the earlier table) — suggesting Black graduates’ disconnection, unlike American Indian graduates’, is more evenly split between the two mechanisms rather than dominated by either one.
SpecialEdStatus (χ² = 145.661, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.067)
Persistent no-record: 25.7% vs. 19.7% — a 6.0-point gap, almost exactly matching the 6.1-point gap found for non-sustained employment. This is the clearest example of a variable whose blended effect (V = 0.113, the strongest demographic relationship in the whole project) splits roughly evenly between the two mechanisms, rather than being dominated by one — genuinely different from every other demographic variable examined so far.
Gender (χ² = 8.890, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.016, p = 0.031)
Barely significant, and the weakest relationship in this entire table. Persistent no-record: 21.2% (male) vs. 20.8% (female) — a negligible 0.4-point gap. This confirms the prediction dramatically: Gender’s disconnection effect, which strengthened to become the strongest relationship in the non-sustained table (V = 0.091), essentially disappears here. Gender’s disadvantage in this population is specifically and almost exclusively about employment instability, not record-absence.
Economic Status (χ² = 34.876, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.033)
Also weak, and the direction is worth flagging: persistent no-record is slightly lower for economically disadvantaged individuals (20.4% vs. 21.5%). Combined with economic status’s relatively stronger relationship with non-sustained employment (V = 0.081 in the earlier table), this confirms Economic status is, like Gender, primarily an employment-instability variable rather than a record-absence one.

Substantive Pattern — this is now a fully resolved, three-way finding
Every demographic variable examined across all three outcome specifications now has a clear, specific mechanism attached to it, rather than a single blended “disconnection” story:

Gender and Economic status operate almost entirely through genuine employment instability.
English learner status and Non-English home operate almost entirely through disappearance from Minnesota’s employment record.
SpecialEdStatus is genuinely mixed, splitting close to evenly between the two mechanisms.
RaceEthnicity is group-specific: American Indian graduates’ disparity is disproportionately about record-absence, while Black graduates’ disparity is more evenly split — meaning “racial disparity in workforce disconnection” is not a single phenomenon even within this one demographic variable.

Connecting back to the open question
This is meaningful, if still indirect, evidence on what “No MN employment record” represents. The fact that it’s overwhelmingly concentrated among English learners and non-English-home students — populations where out-of-state relocation (including to a different state or country) or gaps tied to language/documentation barriers to formal employment are both plausible — leans toward “no record” capturing something like migration or exit from Minnesota’s tracked labor market, rather than simple non-participation in the labor force generally. That’s still a hypothesis, not a conclusion, but it’s now supported by a specific, consistent pattern across two closely related variables rather than a single ambiguous finding.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
High school characteristics
Overall pattern — partial confirmation, one genuine surprise
The categorical variables here behave as predicted from the non-sustained-only table: both edr and Dem_Desc strengthen somewhat when isolated to no-record status. But the two continuous local-economy variables produce a genuine surprise — neither reaches significance here either, meaning their weak blended-table significance doesn’t cleanly belong to either mechanism. This is worth sitting with rather than smoothing over.
Dem_Desc (χ² = 44.294, df = 6, Cramér’s V = 0.026, p < 0.001)
Strengthens modestly relative to both prior tables (blended: 0.014; non-sustained-only: 0.019). Persistent no-record shows a small gradient: Entirely urban (19.5%) < Town/rural mix (20.4%) < Urban/town/rural mix (22.3%) — a 2.8-point spread, still modest in absolute terms but the clearest pattern this variable has shown across any of the three outcome specifications.
edr (χ² = 37.195, df = 3, Cramér’s V = 0.034, p < 0.001)
This is the clearest confirmation of the prediction in this table. edr was significant but weak in the blended measure (V = 0.021), then dropped to complete non-significance in the non-sustained-only table (p = 0.692) — and now returns as the strongest relationship in this HS-characteristics group (V = 0.034). EDR 10 shows higher persistent no-record status than EDR 9 (21.3% vs. 20.4%), and — more tellingly — EDR 9 shows notably higher “Never no-record” (58.4% vs. 54.9%). This confirms that edr’s original blended relationship was entirely a no-record phenomenon, with zero contribution from employment instability, a clean example of the pattern this whole three-way comparison was designed to detect.
avg.unemp.rate (F = 1.677, df = 3/32,874, p = 0.170)
Not significant — and this breaks the pattern rather than confirming it. This variable was weakly significant in the blended table (p = 0.023) and non-significant in the non-sustained-only table (p = 0.161). If the prediction held, it should have reached significance here. It didn’t. Local unemployment rate shows no clear relationship with either specific disconnection mechanism — its weak blended-table significance appears to have been a product of very large sample size rather than a real, attributable effect belonging to either pathway.
avg.wages.pct.state (F = 0.926, df = 3/32,874, p = 0.427)
Also not significant, and also breaks the pattern the same way. Weakly significant in the blended table (p = 0.030), non-significant in non-sustained-only (p = 0.608), and now non-significant here as well. Same conclusion as unemployment rate: this variable’s blended significance does not appear to be genuinely attributable to either the non-sustained or no-record mechanism specifically.

Substantive Pattern
This table requires a genuine revision to the framework established over the last several tables. It’s not simply true that every blended relationship decomposes cleanly into “belongs to non-sustained” or “belongs to no-record” — for avg.unemp.rate and avg.wages.pct.state, the honest conclusion is that their weak blended-table significance likely reflects the very large sample size (N = 32,878) crossing the p < 0.05 threshold on noise, rather than a real relationship with disconnection through either specific pathway. This is a useful, if less exciting, finding in its own right: local labor-market context at the high-school level shows essentially no meaningful bivariate relationship with any disconnection outcome examined in this entire analysis, however the outcome is sliced.
By contrast, edr and Dem_Desc both confirm the broader pattern nicely — modest geography effects that are specifically about record-presence, not employment stability.
Connecting back to the open question
edr’s clean no-record-driven pattern adds a small but real data point to the “what does no-record mean” question: if leaving the region (or the specific EDR) for elsewhere is part of what drives no-record status, a real EDR-level difference in no-record rates is consistent with a migration-related interpretation, though it’s a modest effect and shouldn’t be overweighted on its own.
